power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: The Effectiveness of Single-session Interventions for Anxiety and Depressive Disorders in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
table.research_questions: We anticipate that SSIs will be superior to control conditions and similar in effectiveness to other multi-session psychotherapies in reducing psychological problems. Based on a previous meta-analysis examining SSIs for psychiatric issues in children and adolescents, we expect to find a small to moderate effect size (Schleider & Weisz, 2017).
table.study_type: Meta-Analysis - A systematic review of published studies.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: This meta-analysis will use data from published studies.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Data will be collected from published randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of SSIs on adult psychological problems.
The included RCTs should meet the following criteria: 
1.	Be published in English
2.	Participants are adults (at least 18 years old)
3.	Participants have elevated symptoms or diagnoses of an anxiety disorder (e.g., Panic/agoraphobia, GAD, SAD/Social phobia) or a depressive disorder (e.g., MDD, postpartum depression)
4.	A psychological intervention is compared to a control group (e.g., waiting list, care-as-usual, other controls) or to another psychological intervention (e.g., CBT, behavioral activation, non-directive supportive therapy, etc.)
5.	The intervention is an SSI (SSIs are defined here as a single treatment completed in one day with a clinic/program, including one day sessions that involve multiple “modules”, and including both self-guided and therapist-guided interventions)
6.	Effect sizes of target problem are stated or computable from the available data
SSIs for specific phobia have already been established as effective. For this reason, studies on specific phobia will be excluded from this meta-analysis.
Participants with co-occurring psychiatric symptoms will not be excluded. No restrictions on recruitment method or setting will be applied (i.e., can be recruited from outpatient clinics, hospitals, inpatient clinics, etc.).
table.sample_size: A recent meta-analysis on SSIs for all youth psychiatric problems included 51 RCTs (Schleider & Weisz, 2017). Since we are only investigating problems related to anxiety and depression in adults, we can reasonably expect to include around 30 studies.
table.measured_variables:
We will examine characteristics of the participants (i.e., mean age, recruitment method, presence of psychiatric comorbidity), of the interventions (i.e., intervention type, targeted problem, control condition, session duration) and of the study (i.e., year of publication; country) 
We will also assess risk of bias according to the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool version 2 (i.e., sequence generation; allocation concealment; blinding of participants and personnel; blinding of outcome assessment; incomplete outcome data; selective Reporting). 
Lastly, we will extract data to calculate effect sizes based on both pre- and post-intervention data (i.e., means, standard deviations (SDs), and number of participants at baseline and post-intervention in the experimental and control conditions). Since trials will likely have smaller sample sizes, Hedges’ g will be used to adjust for small sample size bias. We will calculate Hedges’ g as the differential mean change between the treatment and control group’s baseline to post-intervention scores. Since we will only include RCT’s, we assume each trial to be balanced on baseline variables. So, if trials have sufficiently large sample sizes, we should find the same effects using both baseline and post-intervention data as when we use the baseline data alone. 

If the means and SDs are not reported in a trial, we will use change scores. If change scores are not available, we will convert binary outcomes to Hedges’ g. If this data is also not available, we will use other statistics (e.g., p value, t value) to compute the effect size. If there is not sufficient data to calculate the effect size, it will be excluded from the meta-analysis.
table.inference_criteria: Between-group significance testing will be based on the standard p<.05 criteria (95% confidence interval).
table.missing_data_handling: We will not have missing data, as studies with necessary information missing will not be included in the study.
table.exploratory_analyses: Moderator analyses on the characteristics of the participants, interventions, and studies (see section Measure variables).
table.statistical_tests:
This meta-analysis will investigate the effectiveness of SSIs for anxiety and depressive problems in adults. All analyses in this project will be conducted in R using the metapsyTools package in R (version 4.1.1) and Rstudio (version 1.1.463 for Mac) (Borenstein et al., 2017). This package incorporates the meta, metafor, and dmetar packages (Borenstein et al., 2009).

For the main analyses, two separate pooled analyses will be conducted. The first analysis will pool the effect sizes of trials comparing SSIs with psychotherapies (i.e., CBT, behavioral activation, third-wave therapies, and non-directive supportive therapy). The second analysis will pool the effect sizes of trials comparing SSIs to control conditions (i.e., waitlist, care-as-usual, and other controls such as psychological placebo/attention control, or general information about depression/anxiety). 

Both analyses will be pooled using Hedges’ g to determine the overall treatment effect. As we expect a substantial heterogeneity between studies, we will use a random-effects model for pooling studies in all analyses. The primary outcome will be the targeted problem (primary problem targeted by intervention). The effect size level will be used for comparison of trials. Effect sizes of 0.2 are considered small, 0.5 are moderate, and 0.8 are large (Cohen, 1988). Effect sizes will be computed using post-treatment data.

To quantify heterogeneity between studies, we will compute the I² statistic and its 95% confidence intervals, as well as the prediction interval. To test for publication bias, we will use Duval and Tweedie’s trim and fill procedure, the Egger's intercept test, and visually inspect the funnel plot for asymmetry (Duval, 2000; Egger et al. 1997).

Then, contingent on the number and characteristics of the included studies, we may conduct subgroup or sensitivity analyses based on the following factors:
1.	Intervention Type (e.g., CBT)
2.	Problem Type
3.	Problem Severity (i.e., meets diagnostic criteria vs. subthreshold symptoms)
4.	Intervention Format (e.g., group, individual, etc.)
5.	Delivery (e.g., online vs. in-person)
6.	Guidance (self-guided vs. therapist guided)
7.	Target group (e.g., older adults, students, medical population, etc.)
8.	Control comparison (e.g., waiting list, care as usual, other control, other psychotherapy)
9.	Instrument
10.	Rating (e.g., clinician, self-report)
11.	Session duration 
12.	Comorbid disorder (yes/no)
13.	Mean age
These subgroup analyses will be conducted using the mixed effects model, which assumes random effects within subgroups, and fixed effects between subgroups. 

Moreover, if possible, the following sensitivity analyses will be conducted: 
1)	Exclusion of study/studies with outlying effect size(s) (i.e., study effect size does not overlap with the 95% CI of the pooled effect size)
2)	Exclusion of studies with high risk of bias

table.study_design_overview:
We will conduct a meta-analysis examining the effectiveness of SSIs for adult anxiety and depressive problems based on published randomized control trials.

Two pre-existing databases of randomized controlled trials on psychotherapies for depression and anxiety will be utilized for the eligibility screening, and are reported in detail elsewhere (Papola et al., 2022; Cuijpers et al., 2022). The databases were created through comprehensive literature searches of major bibliographic databases, including PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase, and the Cochrane Library.

In addition to using the meta-analytic anxiety and depression databases (Papola et al., 2022; Cuijpers et al., 2022), we will perform additional, tailored systematic searches in PubMed, EBSCO PsycArticles, Embase and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). We will also search through the references of previous meta-analyses and through the references of the trials meeting eligibility criteria.

The full search string for PubMed is:
(("single-session"[Title/Abstract] OR "single-session"[Title/Abstract] OR "one-session"[Title/Abstract] OR "one-session"[Title/Abstract] OR "one-at-a-time"[Title/Abstract]) AND ("psychotherapy"[Title/Abstract] OR "treatment"[Title/Abstract] OR "intervention"[Title/Abstract] OR "therap*"[Title/Abstract]) AND "adult*"[Title/Abstract]) AND (randomizedcontrolledtrial[Filter])
Hits = 175

All records will be imported to Endnote. After exclusion of duplicate records, two independent researchers will screen for titles and abstracts. All trials meeting inclusion criteria as per at least one of the researchers will be retrieved as full text. Then, the full-text articles will be screened by two independent researchers for eligibility based on the relevant inclusion/exclusion criteria (see Data collection procedures). Any disputes will be resolved through discussion and if needed, by consulting a third researcher.

text.text: Objective: Single-session interventions (SSIs) have been proposed as a scalable approach to reduce anxiety and depressive symptoms; however, evidence for adults remains limited.
This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating SSIs relative to inactive or minimal-control conditions.
Method: A systematic search identified adult RCTs.
Outcomes were analyzed separately for anxiety and depression using three-level random-effects meta-analytic models.
Effects were pooled across 1-13 weeks and within short-term (1-3 weeks) and medium-term (4-13 weeks) follow-up windows.
Results: Twenty-one RCTs (N = 7,035) contributed 53 outcome-level effect sizes.
Across 1-13 weeks, SSIs were associated with significant reductions in anxiety symptoms (g = -0.66, 95% CI [-0.98, -0.34]) and depressive symptoms (g = -0.49, 95% CI [-0.84, -0.13]).
At 1-3 weeks, effects were significant for anxiety symptoms (g = -0.80, 95% CI [-1.24, -0.36]), but not depressive symptoms (g = -0.78, 95% CI [-1.78, 0.22]).
At 4-13 weeks, effects were significant for both depressive symptoms (g = -0.29, 95% CI [-0.55, -0.02]) and anxiety symptoms (g = -0.48, 95% CI [-0.93, -0.02]).

Heterogeneity was high, prediction intervals were wide, publication bias was detected for anxiety outcomes at 1-13 and 1-3 weeks and for depression at 1-13 weeks, and most studies had some concerns or high risk of bias.
Conclusions: SSIs may reduce anxiety and depressive symptoms over the short-to-medium term in adults.
Substantial heterogeneity, limited trial availability, publication bias, and risk of bias constrain confidence in the magnitude and generalizability of these effects.
Rigorous trials with extended follow-up are needed to clarify effect durability and further inform the role within routine care.
This meta-analysis suggests that psychological interventions designed to be delivered in a single session may reduce anxiety and depressive symptoms in adults over the short to medium term.

These interventions may provide an additional brief option within mental health care, but future research is needed to determine how durable their effects are, for whom they work, and how they should be implemented in routine practice.
The findings should be interpreted cautiously because the included studies differed substantially and many had methodological limitations.

text.text: In the present review, we use SSI in a narrower operational sense to refer to structured, evidence-informed psychological interventions designed and evaluated as single-session interventions for adult anxiety or depressive symptoms.
For example, an SSI for depression may target behavioral activation or cognitive restructuring, whereas an SSI for anxiety may target exposure, anxiety sensitivity, or catastrophic appraisals.

Delivery formats may range from clinician-led to digital self-guided programs or blended models with minimal non-therapeutic follow-up (i.e., any post-session contact limited to reminders, assessment completion, logistical communication, or non-clinical check-ins, without introducing new therapeutic content, individualized clinical feedback, skills training, or additional treatment sessions).
While not intended to replace longer-term psychotherapy in complex or chronic cases, SSIs can serve multiple roles within mental health care systems.

They may function as standalone treatments for mild to moderate symptoms, as adjuncts to ongoing therapy, or as accessible entry points for individuals who might otherwise remain untreated (Hoyt et al., 2018; Kazdin, 2017; Schleider et al., 2022).

text.text: Despite these encouraging findings for the general effectiveness of SSIs across populations, critical gaps persist in the literature.

Most prior reviews evaluating SSI effectiveness have been narrative rather than quantitative, have concentrated on youth populations, or have combined heterogeneous outcomes across diverse symptom domains (Schleider & Weisz, 2017; Schleider et al., 2022).

text.text: Moreover, although early post-intervention outcomes are frequently reported, the existing literature has not yet established a consistent or fine-grained temporal differentiation of SSI effects.
Follow-up assessments vary widely in timing across studies, and prior syntheses have typically aggregated early outcomes rather than systematically comparing adjacent post-intervention windows.

This distinction is relevant because broader SSI evidence suggests that effects may vary by follow-up length, with larger average effects observed at very short follow-up than at later assessments (Schleider et al., 2025).

text.text: As a result, post-intervention outcomes are often treated collectively as a pragmatic indicator of SSI impact, even though symptom trajectories within and beyond this window remain insufficiently resolved.
Separating adjacent shortterm and more distal assessments may therefore offer additional insight into potential temporal patterns without presupposing their presence.
Against this backdrop, evidence regarding how SSI effects unfold over time in adults with anxiety and depression remains limited.

Given the high prevalence and disabling burden of these conditions in adulthood, and the reality that many adults receive little or no care beyond a single encounter, strengthening the adult evidence base is particularly important.

Doing so would help determine whether SSIs can be considered an evidence-based approach for anxiety and depression and clarify their potential role in expanding access to effective psychological interventions (Kazdin, 2017; Schleider et al., 2025).

text.text: Related brief-intervention formats were considered eligible only when they were explicitly designed as single-session interventions, targeted anxiety and/or depressive symptoms in adults, and met the review's randomized controlled trial and comparator criteria.

Accordingly, this systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of singlesession interventions (SSIs) on adult anxiety and depressive symptoms, relative to inactive or minimal-control conditions, operationalized as waitlist, no intervention, usual care, or minimal, nonspecific, or placebo-like comparators; structured psychological treatments evaluated as alternative interventions were excluded.
Analyses were conducted separately for anxiety and depression.
For each outcome domain, effect sizes were first pooled across all available post-intervention assessments within the short-to-medium term.
Subsequently, domain-specific effects were estimated separately across adjacent follow-up windows to assess potential temporal variation in SSI effectiveness.

Based on prior evidence suggesting that SSI effects may be strongest shortly after intervention delivery and may attenuate over time (Cape et al., 2010; Schleider et al., 2025), we expected that SSIs would yield significant reductions in anxiety and depressive symptoms across the available short-to-medium-term post-intervention period, and that effect size estimates would be descriptively larger at earlier than later follow-up assessments.

A detailed rationale for all protocol refinements is provided in Supplement D.
A comprehensive literature search was conducted on May 5, 2026.

To identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs), we first screened two curated databases maintained by the Meta-analytic Research Domains (MARDs) initiative: the Metapsy Depression Database and the Metapsy Anxiety Database (Cuijpers et al., 2023; www.metapsy.org).

text.text: These living databases are systematically updated and include all published RCTs of evidence-based psychological interventions for depression (updated quarterly) and anxiety (updated annually).

Recognizing that SSIs may be underrepresented or inconsistently labeled in these broader psychotherapy databases, we additionally developed a tailored search strategy using keyword combinations specifically related to SSIs and brief psychotherapies.
This targeted search was run across four major electronic databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials).
The full search string and syntax for each database are provided in the Supplementary Material.

In addition to database and register searches, records were identified through consultation with subject-matter experts, including researchers who had contributed to trials or data resources relevant to this review; records identified this way underwent the same eligibility screening as records identified through the search strategies above.

For trials with published reports insufficient for effect-size calculation, deidentified individual participant data (IPD) were sought, either from publicly archived data repositories or by direct request to study authors.

Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) employed a randomized controlled trial (RCT) design; (2) included adult participants, defined as samples restricted to participants aged 18 years or older, with either a formal diagnosis of anxiety or depression based on DSM or ICD criteria or clinically significant symptoms as determined by standardized instruments; (3) evaluated an SSI derived from an evidence-informed psychotherapeutic approach, defined as a recognizable psychological treatment model with prior empirical support for anxiety, depression, or related internalizing symptoms, from which the SSI delivered at least one identifiable therapeutic component; (4) delivered the intervention in one primary therapeutic session, with optional non-therapeutic follow-up only when post-session contact was limited to reminders, assessment prompts, logistical communication, or brief non-clinical check-ins and did not introduce new therapeutic content, individualized clinical feedback, skills training, or booster intervention material; (5) compared the SSI with an inactive or minimal-control condition, operationalized as waitlist, no intervention, usual care, or a minimal, nonspecific, or placebo-like comparator, such as a reading task, study-skills module, physical-health education, or expressive writing.

Comparator conditions could be matched to the SSI in length, format, attention, or activity level, but studies were excluded when the comparator was a structured psychological treatment evaluated as an alternative intervention; (6) reported post-intervention anxiety and/or depressive symptom outcomes using psychometrically established instruments, defined as standardized symptom measures for which prior published psychometric evaluations demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity in relevant or comparable populations, with sufficient data for effect-size computation.

For trials in which arm-level eligibility could not be determined from the published report, for example, trials evaluating several intervention variants against a shared comparator, eligibility was assessed separately for each arm against the criteria above, and study authors were contacted for clarification when necessary.
Only arms independently judged eligible were retained; each eligible arm was treated as a separate intervention-control contrast for data extraction and analysis.
Two researchers independently screened all abstracts and full texts.
Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer.

Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool ( Sterne et   al., 2019), which evaluates potential bias across five domains: the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selection of the reported results.

For trials contributing multiple eligible arms compared against a single shared control condition, risk of bias was assessed once at the trial level and applied to all contributing arms.
Two researchers independently assessed the risk of bias for each included study.
Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer.
Two researchers independently extracted data using a standardized template.
Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third author.
We extracted three types of data: study characteristics, intervention and comparator characteristics, and outcome data.

Study characteristics included publication year, country, recruitment setting (academic, healthcare, or community), recruitment strategy, target condition (anxiety or depression), diagnostic status, and demographic characteristics,
We extracted means and standard deviations from intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses when available; otherwise, completer-only data were extracted.

For each study, we identified eligible intervention-control contrasts, defined as contrasts between a single-session intervention (SSI) and inactive or minimal-control conditions When studies included multiple eligible SSI or control arms, each qualifying SSIcontrol pairing was treated as a separate intervention-control contrast.
From each intervention-control contrast, outcome data were extracted for each eligible symptom instrument reported at post-intervention assessments.
When multiple instruments were reported within the same contrast, data from each instrument were extracted separately and treated as distinct outcome-level effect sizes.
Thus, effect sizes were derived at the outcome level, based on instrument-specific data within each intervention-control contrast.

Only total scores from psychometrically established instruments (i.e., standardized symptom measures with published evidence of reliability and validity for assessing anxiety or depressive symptoms, excluding ad hoc, single-item, author-created, or non-symptom measures without prior psychometric evaluation, e.g., BDI-II, PHQ-9, GAD-7) were included.
Outcomes were classified by symptom domain (anxiety or depression).

For each outcome-level effect size derived from an intervention-control contrast, standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) were calculated as the difference in mean postintervention scores between intervention and control groups, divided by the pooled standard deviation and corrected for small-sample bias (Hedges, 1981).

text.text: Negative values reflected lower symptom scores in the SSI group relative to controls; conventional benchmarks are approximately -0.20, -0.50, and -0.80 for small, moderate, and large effects, respectively (Cohen, 1977).

text.text: For studies that did not report arm-level post-intervention means and standard deviations in the format required for the standardization procedure above, but for which deidentified individual participant data (IPD) were available, effect sizes were derived by reproducing the study's primary analytic model (e.g., a longitudinal mixed-effects model of the relevant outcome) and extracting the model-estimated between-group coefficient and its standard error at the corresponding post-intervention assessment.

This coefficient and its standard error were standardized using the pooled available-case standard deviation at that assessment, computed directly from the IPD, and corrected for small-sample bias (Hedges, 1981), consistent with the standardization approach applied to all other included effect sizes.
Where a study's primary model was reproduced in this way, the resulting coefficients were checked against those reported in the original publication or associated analysis materials before use.
IPD reanalyses were conducted in R using mixed-effects modeling packages (e.g., lme4, lmerTest).
All eligible post-intervention follow-up assessments were extracted.
The primary post-intervention window was defined as 1-13 weeks (hereafter: the short-to-medium-term window), reflecting the range of eligible follow-up assessments available in the included studies.
Within this window, outcome-level effect sizes were grouped into two pragmatic, data-informed intervals: 1-3 weeks and 4-13 weeks.

These intervals were used to distinguish more proximal from later assessments while preserving sufficient outcome-level effect sizes within each analytic window; they were not intended to represent established clinical thresholds.

For studies reporting more than one eligible follow-up assessment within the 1-13 week post-intervention period, each time point was extracted separately and assigned to the corresponding analytic window.

Studies with assessments in both windows could therefore contribute to both the 1-3 week and 4-13 week analyses; dependency among multiple effect sizes from the same study was handled using the three-level model.
Studies reporting only one eligible post-intervention assessment within the 1-13 week window contributed that single effect size to the corresponding analytic interval.

All analyses were conducted using R (version 4.2.2) and RStudio, employing the metapsyTools package (Harrer et al., 2022), which builds on functionality from established meta-analysis packages, including metafor, meta, and dmetar.

text.text: Because several studies contributed more than one outcome-level effect size, effect sizes from the same study or intervention-comparator contrast could not be treated as statistically independent.

We therefore used three-level correlated-and-hierarchical-effects (CHE) random-effects metaanalytic models (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2022), which estimate sampling variability at the effect-size level, dependency among effect sizes within studies or contrasts, and betweenstudy heterogeneity.
text.formatted: We therefore used three-level correlated-and-hierarchical-effects (CHE) random-effects metaanalytic models (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2022), which estimate sampling variability at the effect-size level, dependency among effect sizes within studies or contrasts, and betweenstudy heterogeneity.

text.text: Robust variance estimation was used to obtain standard errors and confidence intervals that account for this dependency structure.

An intra-study correlation of ρ = .60 was specified for dependent outcome-level effect sizes derived from the same construct (e.g., repeated assessments of the same outcome), and an additional correlation of φ = .90 was specified for hierarchically nested effect sizes (e.g., multiple intervention arms compared against a single shared control condition).

These parameters reflect the assumed correlation structure among effect sizes derived from the same study or contrast and primarily affects the estimation of standard errors and confidence intervals rather than the substantive direction of the pooled effect.
Meta-analyses were conducted separately for anxiety and depression.
For each outcome domain, effect sizes were pooled across the overall 1-13 week post-intervention window and separately within the 1-3 week and 4-13 week windows.

For any outcome domain and analytic window in which one included study contributed a substantially larger number of effect sizes, or effect sizes of substantially greater statistical precision, than the remaining included studies, the primary meta-analysis was additionally repeated with that study's contributed effect sizes excluded, to evaluate whether the pooled estimate and its statistical significance were disproportionately driven by that study.

Heterogeneity was assessed by calculating the I² statistic (Higgins & Thompson, 2002; Rücker et al., 2008) and its 95% confidence interval, which estimate the proportion of variance not attributable to sampling error.

text.text: I² values of 0%, 25%, 50%, and 75% represent no, low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins & Thompson, 2002).

text.text: In line with the three-level model structure, we applied a multilevel extension of I² that partitions variance into heterogeneity arising from differences within studies (level 2) and from variability between studies (level 3).
In addition, between-study heterogeneity variance (τ²) was estimated using restricted maximum likelihood.
Prediction intervals (PI) were calculated to indicate the range in which the true effect sizes of comparable future studies are expected to fall.

Numbers needed to treat (NNTs) were calculated from Hedges' g, assuming a control group event rate of 20%, to convert standardized mean differences into NNTs for binary interpretation (Furukawa & Leucht, 2011).

text.text: Sensitivity analyses (i.e., outlier detection, publication bias tests, and bias adjustment methods) were conducted using the combined (two-level) random-effects model.

These procedures were not applied to the three-level model because standard implementations of these diagnostics and bias-adjustment methods are more straightforward for two-level models and are less established for dependent, multilevel effect-size structures.
Outliers were defined as outcome-level effect sizes whose 95% confidence intervals did not overlap with the pooled effect size and were excluded in a subsequent effect-size recalculation.

Publication bias was assessed using Egger's test of the intercept (Egger et al., 1997), but only in meta-analyses including at least 10 studies, in line with recommended thresholds (Sterne et al., 2011).

text.text: The 21 included studies enrolled a total of 7,035 participants.

Fifteen studies (71.4%) delivered the SSI in a face-to-face format, three studies (14.3%) used guided online SSIs, and three studies (14.3%) used unguided online SSIs.

text.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized findings from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining single-session interventions (SSIs) for adult anxiety or depression compared with inactive or minimal-control conditions.
In line with our expectations, significant SSI effects were observed for both anxiety (g = -0.66) and depression (g = -0.49) across the full follow-up period (1-13 weeks post-intervention).

Consistent with our expectation that effects would be descriptively larger at earlier than later follow-up assessments, point estimates were larger at 1-3 weeks than at 4-13 weeks for both anxiety (g = -0.80 vs. -0.48) and depression (g = -0.78 vs. -0.29).

This pattern reached statistical significance at both windows for anxiety, but only at the 4-13 week window for depression; the 1-3 week depression estimate, while descriptively the largest observed, had a wide confidence interval spanning the null (95% CI [-1.78, 0.22]), likely reflecting the small number of contributing studies (k = 5) at that window.
Sensitivity analyses yielded broadly similar results across conditions and follow-up windows.
The depression estimates showed comparatively greater sensitivity to the inclusion of one large trial, discussed further below.

These follow-up windows should be interpreted as pragmatic analytic groupings rather than established clinical thresholds, reflecting the distribution of available assessment points in the included studies.
Overall, interpretation of our findings warrants caution.

Although the non-significant estimates were in the expected direction, their confidence intervals included the null, i.e., the pooled estimate was statistically inconclusive and compatible with a range of possible effects.
Therefore, these findings should be interpreted as inconclusive rather than as evidence of (in)effectiveness.

Across most analyses, heterogeneity was substantial and prediction intervals were wide, indicating that pooled effects represent averages across interventions, populations, and trial designs that differ in potentially meaningful ways (e.g., intervention content, delivery mode, target populations, and control condition stringency).
The small number of independent studies limited the extent to which these sources of heterogeneity could be examined statistically.

Subgroup analyses based on small numbers of studies are often underpowered, and nonsignificant subgroup differences would not establish that effects are equivalent across categories (Harrer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Subgroup analyses based on small numbers of studies are often underpowered, and nonsignificant subgroup differences would not establish that effects are equivalent across categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Harrer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such heterogeneity implies that true effects vary considerably across studies, which reduces the precision of pooled estimates and may contribute to non-significant findings in specific follow-up windows despite non-zero point estimates.

Although this diversity underscores the conceptual flexibility and adaptability of SSIs, it necessarily limits the extent to which any single pooled effect can be generalized to specific populations or implementation contexts.
In addition, evidence of publication bias was detected for anxiety outcomes at both the 1-13 week and 1-3 week windows, suggesting that studies with null or smaller effects may be underrepresented.
Evidence of publication bias was also detected for depression at 1-13 weeks when Kaveladze et al. (2026) was included; no such evidence was found at 4-13 weeks.

Because Egger's test requires at least 10 independent studies, publication-bias diagnostics could not be conducted for any depression subset excluding this trial, nor for the anxiety 4-13-week or depression 1-3-week windows, and the presence of bias in these narrower subsets cannot be excluded.

Moreover, only two included trials were judged to be at low risk of bias; most studies raised some concerns or were rated as high risk due to factors such as lack of preregistration or inadequate allocation concealment.
Collectively, these factors may both inflate pooled effect estimates and obscure reliable detection of effects within narrower time windows.
A related consideration concerns the influence of a single large trial identified through consultation with subject-matter experts (Kaveladze et al., 2026).

text.text: This trial had been completed as of our search date but was not captured by the database searches.
It contributed a disproportionate share of the available depression effect sizes (40-53%, depending on window) and was markedly more statistically precise than the remaining depression trials.

When this trial was excluded, pooled depression effects were larger at both the 1-13 week window (g = -0.56 vs. -0.49) and the 4-13 week window (g = -0.42 vs. -0.29), though estimates remained statistically significant either way.
This suggests the depression estimates reported here are, to some extent, attenuated by this trial relative to what the smaller, earlier trials alone would suggest.

Because this trial was self-guided, delivered entirely online, and recruited a large community sample, its smaller observed effect may reflect differences in population, delivery format, or engagement rather than a true difference in intervention efficacy; conversely, its larger sample and low risk of bias may make it a more precise, less inflated estimate of the true effect than the smaller trials it is being compared against.

Both interpretations remain speculative given that only one trial of this scale is currently available, and replication in similarly large, low-risk-of-bias adult SSI trials will be needed to adjudicate between them.
A post hoc analysis of within-control-group change offers a complementary perspective on this attenuation.

Across the 10 depression trials with an eligible control arm, control conditions showed a statistically significant improvement from baseline to postintervention on average (g = -0.40, 95% CI [-0.67, -0.12]), indicating that participants in inactive or minimal-control conditions also tended to improve over time, independent of any SSI-specific benefit.

This is consistent with the broader observation that between-group effect sizes partly reflect the extent to which control conditions themselves are associated with improvement (e.g., regression to the mean, natural symptom fluctuation, or nonspecific effects of trial participation), rather than solely reflecting intervention efficacy.

A moderator analysis found no evidence that control-arm improvement in Kaveladze et al. (2026) differed from that of the other depression trials' control arms (QM(1) = 0.10, p = .755), suggesting its smaller between-group effect is not attributable to an unusually large improvement in its control condition specifically.

Nevertheless, the present findings align with prior work supporting the therapeutic potential of single-session interventions in adult populations (e.g., Odgers et al., 2022; Schleider et al., 2025).

However, effect sizes reported in youth samples have generally been smaller (e.g., anxiety g ≈ 0.56; depression g ≈ 0.21; Schleider & Weisz, 2017; Schleider et al., 2025).

text.text: One plausible explanation, among other factors, may be that adult SSI trials more frequently enroll treatment-seeking individuals with clinically significant distress, whereas youth SSI studies often target preventive or subclinical populations, thereby limiting the magnitude of observable symptom change.

This interpretation is consistent with broader psychotherapy research indicating larger effects in higher-severity samples compared with preventive or lower-intensity intervention contexts (e.g., Driessen et al., 2010).

text.text: Several strengths of the present review warrant consideration.

First, to our knowledge, this meta-analysis provides the first quantitative synthesis explicitly focused on short-tomedium-term effects of single-session interventions for adult anxiety and depression, addressing a gap in the SSI literature that has primarily emphasized youth populations or aggregated outcomes across symptom domains in adults (e.g., Schleider & Weisz, 2017; Schleider et al., 2025).
text.formatted: First, to our knowledge, this meta-analysis provides the first quantitative synthesis explicitly focused on short-tomedium-term effects of single-session interventions for adult anxiety and depression, addressing a gap in the SSI literature that has primarily emphasized youth populations or aggregated outcomes across symptom domains in adults (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Schleider & Weisz, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Schleider et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Second, by examining short-term and medium-term outcomes separately for each symptom domain, the review offers a more differentiated, domainspecific characterization of SSI effects across adjacent post-intervention windows.

Third, despite the modest number of available trials (k = 21), the included studies encompassed a range of therapeutic approaches, delivery formats, and adult age groups while adhering to a common SSI framework, enhancing the relevance of the findings to contemporary implementation contexts.

Fourth, the use of three-level random-effects models constitutes a methodological strength, allowing for appropriate handling of dependency among multiple effect sizes within studies and more accurate estimation of uncertainty.

Finally, situating the observed short-to-medium-term effects in relation to both youth SSI research and the broader psychotherapy literature helps contextualize adult SSI effects within established evidence on brief psychological interventions.
However, several limitations constrain the conclusions that can be drawn from this synthesis.

The number of included randomized controlled trials remains small, with most studies conducted between 2012 and 2019 and relatively few published in recent years, indicating a slow accumulation of evidence in adult SSI research, though the total available sample size has grown substantially with the addition of one large 2026 trial.

Moreover, the majority of trials were conducted in high-income countries and enrolled predominantly female, highly educated participants, which limits the generalizability of the findings to more diverse populations and to low-and middle-income settings (WHO, 2023; Yan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Moreover, the majority of trials were conducted in high-income countries and enrolled predominantly female, highly educated participants, which limits the generalizability of the findings to more diverse populations and to low-and middle-income settings <ref type="bibr">(WHO, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Yan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Comparator conditions also varied in stringency, ranging from waitlist or no-treatment controls to usual-care and placebo-like conditions.

Although all met the prespecified definition of an inactive or minimal-control condition and none constituted a structured psychological treatment evaluated as an alternative intervention, they may still have differed in nonspecific factors such as contact, expectancy, symptom monitoring, or access to usual services.
Formal interrater reliability statistics could not be reported because the preconsensus screening data required for retrospective calculation were unavailable.

Finally, the within-control-group change analysis (see Meta-analyses and Results) was a post hoc addition prompted by an unexpected pattern in the depression findings rather than a preregistered analysis; its results should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
Beyond these constraints, important questions remain regarding the durability and longer-term implications of SSI effects.

Although short-to-medium-term effects are commonly regarded as a primary therapeutic target of single-session interventions, longerterm outcomes remain essential for clarifying the role of SSIs within stepped-care and population-level mental health systems.

In particular, evidence on whether a subset of individuals maintains clinically meaningful improvement over time would help determine the extent to which SSIs can reduce reliance on more intensive, multisession treatments by addressing needs amenable to brief care.
This perspective aligns with emerging conceptualizations of SSIs as scalable components that complement, rather than replace, traditional services (Schleider et al., 2025).
Future research should aim to address these gaps and strengthen the evidence base for SSIs targeting anxiety and depressive symptoms in adults across several key domains.

First, additional preregistered and methodologically rigorous randomized controlled trials focused on adult anxiety and depression are needed to improve the precision and credibility of effect estimates and to reduce the risk of bias and publication-related inflation evident in the current literature.

Second, trials should incorporate longer follow-up periods and multiple postintervention assessments to more clearly delineate the durability of short-to-medium-term SSI effects on anxiety and depressive symptoms and to characterize symptom trajectories beyond this time frame.
Third, systematic investigation of moderators relevant to adult anxiety and depression will be important for clarifying for whom SSIs are most effective and under which conditions.

Future meta-analyses should examine whether SSI effects vary by intervention and study characteristics, including therapeutic orientation, delivery format, session duration, comparator type, baseline severity, diagnostic status, age, and participant population.

In the present evidence base, these characteristics were too sparsely represented and often closely intertwined to support reliable formal moderator analyses; for example, differences in session duration frequently reflected broader differences in intervention format, content, and intensity.

As the adult SSI literature grows, larger evidence bases will be needed to disentangle these sources of heterogeneity and determine whether observed variation in effects reflects true moderation rather than study-level confounding.
Fourth, future research should examine SSI effects in relation to active comparator conditions.
The present review focused on whether SSIs show symptom effects relative to waitlist, no intervention, usual care, or minimal, nonspecific, or placebo-like comparators.
Such comparators could be matched to the SSI in length, format, attention, or activity level, but structured psychological treatments evaluated as alternative interventions were excluded.
By contrast, activecomparator trials address a distinct comparative question: whether SSIs are superior, equivalent, or noninferior to other active psychological interventions.

This question is particularly relevant for implementation, because SSIs may be valuable not only if they produce larger symptom reductions, but also if they achieve comparable outcomes with lower time burden, lower cost, greater scalability, or easier delivery.
Future meta-analyses should therefore examine active-comparator trials separately once a sufficiently large adult evidence base is available.

Fifth, greater attention to mechanisms of change implicated in anxiety and depression (e.g., skill acquisition, cognitive restructuring, changes in hope or perceived control) would help elucidate how SSIs exert their effects in adult samples and guide optimization of intervention content and delivery.

Sixth, future research should explicitly evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and scalability of SSIs for adult anxiety and depression, particularly in settings where the treatment gap for common mental disorders is most pronounced, such as low-and middle-income countries (Patel et al., 2018; WHO, 2023).

text.text: This section documents and justifies refinements to the preregistered protocol that were implemented after registration but prior to study identification and data extraction, in accordance with PRISMA recommendations for transparent reporting of protocol deviations.
In the preregistered protocol, we planned to include comparisons between single-session interventions (SSIs) and both inactive control conditions and multisession psychotherapies.

Prior to study identification, this scope was refined to include only comparisons between SSIs and inactive control conditions (e.g., waitlist, no treatment, care-as-usual, or information-only controls).
This refinement was motivated by conceptual and methodological considerations.

First, the primary objective of the review was to establish whether SSIs produce measurable symptom reductions for adult anxiety and depression relative to minimal or no intervention, which represents the conventional first step in evaluating the effectiveness of a psychological intervention.

Comparisons with inactive controls provide a clearer estimate of absolute intervention effects and avoid conflating SSI efficacy with differences in treatment intensity, duration, or therapist contact inherent in comparisons with multisession psychotherapies.
Second, preliminary scoping indicated that trials directly comparing SSIs with multisession psychotherapies were rare limiting the interpretability of pooled estimates.
Including such comparisons would likely have introduced substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity without meaningfully advancing the primary research question.

Importantly, this refinement did not alter the core research objective, namely, to evaluate the effectiveness of SSIs for adult anxiety and depression, but rather clarified the comparator framework to align with best practices in intervention evaluation and meta-analytic methodology.
The preregistered protocol specified post-intervention symptom outcomes but did not predefine specific follow-up intervals.

Prior to data extraction, follow-up assessments were operationalized into short-term (1-3 weeks), medium-term (4-13 weeks), and overall (1-13 weeks) intervals, corresponding to an empirically supported proximal post-intervention window.
This decision was informed by both theoretical considerations and the distribution of assessment timepoints across eligible trials.

SSIs are explicitly conceptualized as ultra-brief interventions designed to exert their primary therapeutic effects shortly after intervention delivery, with longer-term outcomes often more variable and dependent on subsequent support or contextual factors.
Consistent with prior SSI meta-analytic work, early postintervention assessments therefore represent the most theoretically appropriate window for evaluating SSI effects.
The preregistered analytic plan specified conventional random-effects meta-analytic models.

Prior to data extraction, this plan was refined to employ three-level random-effects models with robust variance estimation.This refinement was driven by the anticipated data structure of SSI trials, many of which report multiple effect sizes per study (e.g., multiple outcomes, time points, or instruments).
Three-level models allow for appropriate handling of dependency among effect sizes nested within studies, thereby reducing bias in standard errors and improving the accuracy of uncertainty estimates.

Recruitment strategy was coded based on the source of participant recruitment reported by study authors, such as student samples, community recruitment, primary care, outpatient recruitment, other healthcare-based recruitment, or online/crowdsourced recruitment via digital research platforms.

The intervention characteristics extracted were therapeutic orientation, coded according to the primary therapeutic rationale and intervention components described by study authors; delivery mode; session length; format; and assessment time points.

Therapeutic orientation categories included CBT-based, behavioral activation, exposurebased, acceptance-/mindfulness-based, imagery rescripting, narrative, and motivational approaches where applicable.

CBT-based interventions were coded when they followed a multicomponent traditional CBT rationale combining cognitive techniques, such as cognitive restructuring or modification of maladaptive appraisals, with behavioral techniques, such as behavioral experiments or exposure.
Although behavioral activation and exposure are part of the broader CBT tradition, they were coded separately when they constituted the intervention's primary therapeutic rationale and component.

Behavioral activation interventions primarily targeted engagement in rewarding, meaningful, or goal-directed activities, whereas exposure-based interventions primarily involved systematic confrontation with feared stimuli, sensations, or situations.
Acceptance-/mindfulness-based interventions were coded when they emphasized acceptance, mindfulness, values clarification, psychological flexibility, or committed action.
Other approaches, including imagery rescripting, narrative-based interventions, and motivational approaches, were coded according to the primary model specified by the original study authors.
For each eligible comparison, outcome data were extracted for anxiety and depression measures at baseline and at each available post-intervention timepoint.
This included means and standard deviations at baseline and follow-up sample sizes per arm; total number randomized per arm.

Finally, investigation of strategies to sustain gains beyond the short-to-medium-term post-intervention window (e.g., brief booster sessions or digital follow-up components) alongside implementation-focused research addressing training requirements, fidelity, cost-effectiveness, and uptake among adult service users and providers would help inform the integration of SSIs into routine mental health care.In summary, this meta-analysis provides the first quantitative synthesis focused on single-session interventions for adult anxiety and depression, indicating small-to-moderate symptom reductions over the short-to-medium-term following SSI delivery.
While these findings should be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive, they nonetheless suggest that SSIs can yield measurable benefits.

Within this context, SSIs may serve as an accessible option for adults with elevated anxiety or depressive symptoms, as a supplement to ongoing psychological care, or as a temporary source of support for individuals awaiting more intensive treatment.

Their brevity, scalability, and adaptability across delivery formats suggest that SSIs may function as a pragmatic component within existing mental health care pathways, with potential relevance for broader efforts to expand access to evidence-based care and to narrow the global mental health treatment gap.
